events.claim: Through most of the 1800s, many Americans voted with party-printed tickets that were easy to tell apart, often by color, and handed them in where others could see. Louisville and Massachusetts first adopted the government-printed secret Australian ballot in 1888.
events.quote: Parties’ ticket s were typically readily distinguishable from each other, such as by color, and handed to election officials in public view.

also.quote: Louisville, KY, and the State of Massachusetts were the first to adopt it, in 18 88.

events.notes: Congressional Research Service Insight IN12389 (July 5, 2024), read via EveryCRSReport mirror; spacing artifacts ('ticket s', '18 88') are in the mirror text. Low priority item; 99% Invisible not read.

events.claim: The Smithsonian's National Museum of American History holds a 1920 ribbon badge marking a woman's first vote under the 19th Amendment, for the Harding and Coolidge ticket. Its curator calls it the oldest Election Day keepsake in the museum's collection.
events.quote: Badge, Nineteenth Amendment ... ID Number 1986.0640.001 ... overall: 6 1/4 in x 2 1/4 in; 15.875 cm x 5.715 cm

also.quote: Ribbon badge, 1920, "Under the 19th Amendment I Cast My First Vote - Harding/Coolidge." 1986.0640.001. (image courtesy The National Museum of American History)
“We have a button with a ribbon extending down that says ‘I cast my first vote on November 2nd, 1920.’

Badge worn by women supporting Republican presidential candidate Warren G. Harding. The 1920 presidential election was the first in which women from all states could vote after the Nineteenth Amendment enfranchising women was ratified in August, 1920.

events.notes: Record read through the Smithsonian Open Access API (edanmdm:nmah_1051247) because americanhistory.si.edu returned a Cloudflare 500 all session. The record gives title, catalog number 1986.0640.001, yellow textile, and size, but NOT the inscription text and NOT Lancaster. The inscription comes from the Hyperallergic caption and curator Claire Jerry's quote. 'Lancaster, PA' appears only in Wikipedia, which cites Hyperallergic, and Hyperallergic does not say Lancaster: do not use Lancaster. A second NMAH object, nmah_522863 'First Vote Badge' (1980.0606.183, 5 x 2 1/4 in, Pennsylvania, Harding), is a related Republican first-vote badge; its record also lacks inscription text. Metadata is CC0; image rights not stated in the API.

events.claim: A 1950 Miami Herald page is cited as an early mention of "I Have Voted" stickers handed out at Miami polls.
events.quote: The Miami Herald mentioned the distribution of an “I Have Voted” sticker at Miami polls as early as 1950 .

also.quote: Oct 27, 1950, page 25 - The Miami Herald at Newspapers.com

events.notes: The Washington Examiner piece (republished by Colorado Politics, Nov 4, 2024, Annabella Rosciglione) links its '1950' to Newspapers.com image 618114799; the page title in Chrome confirms it is The Miami Herald, Oct 27, 1950, page 25. The page text is behind Newspapers.com's paywall and was not read. The hospital bond vote and time-off-to-vote details from the research appear in no source read: do not use them. Safe wording: 'a 1950 Miami Herald page mentions...', attributed.

events.claim: An October 29, 1982, Miami Herald article described Fort Lauderdale businesses offering discounts to people wearing a voting sticker. Time called it possibly the earliest mention of such a sticker.
events.quote: An Oct. 29, 1982, Miami Herald article may contain the earliest mention of such a sticker

also.quote: One of the first mentions of a sticker that advertised voting can be found in a 1982 Miami Herald article, which noted how small businesses in Fort Lauderdale used the stickers to offer discounts to customers, Time Magazine reported.

events.notes: Time (Olivia B. Waxman, Nov 7, 2016) is the source the others copy. Herald itself not read. Time wrote 'may contain the earliest mention'; it predates the 1950 citation surfacing later, so do not call 1982 'the first'.

events.claim: Voting in Houston in the 1984 presidential election, Vice President George H. W. Bush was given a sticker reading "I Voted Today, Have You?", according to a UPI report that day. Teachers' unions also handed stickers to members that year.
events.quote: The same year, Vice President George H. W. Bush got a sticker that said “I Voted Today — Have You?” in Houston when he cast his ballot in the presidential election in 1984, according to a report that day from the United Press International wire service.

also.quote: Teachers unions offered them to members in 1984 to encourage coworkers to vote.

events.notes: Vox (Libby Nelson, Nov 8, 2016) cites UPI but gives no link; the UPI item was not found in upi.com/Archives searches. The teachers' union line has no cited source. Both are secondary; attribute to Vox citing UPI. Sticker text contains an em dash in the source; on the page write it with a comma or as two lines.

events.claim: In 1985 the Phoenix Board of Realtors made "I voted today" stickers to remind people to vote while a freeway bond issue was on the ballot. Skip Rimsza, the board's president and later Phoenix mayor, and operations director Dennis M. Burke came up with the idea, and Rimsza later claimed they were the first in the country.
events.quote: Rimsza and Dennis M. Burke, the board's operations director then, brainstormed the sticker to spark voter interest. Morning voter turnout at most elections was strong, but the afternoon was always the weakest.

also.quote: Back then, there was a bond issue on the ballot to expand the freeway system.
"We were absolutely the first ones in the country," Rimsza said.
The Phoenix Realtors Association says it started distributing such stickers in Phoenix and Maricopa County
The Phoenix Association of Realtors says 25 million “I Voted” stickers have been distributed since 1985.

events.notes: Source is the Arizona Republic, Nov 8, 2006 (Angela Cara Pancrazio), read via the Wayback Machine. It says 'bond issue'; the research's 'half-cent sales tax' is not in anything read (the 1985 Maricopa freeway vote was a sales tax measure, but no source here says so: don't state it). 'First in the country' is Rimsza's claim and is contradicted by the 1950 and 1982 Herald mentions; present it as a claim. The 2025 azcentral story (Mary Jo Pitzl, Sept 23, 2025) is paywalled; only its first two paragraphs were readable, so designer 'Nikylla Lue Celine' is UNVERIFIED (no search hit anywhere). KJZZ (March 12, 2013) adds the 25 million figure, which is the association's own claim.

events.claim: National Campaign Supply, a Florida company, says it began selling voting stickers in 1986.
events.quote: National Campaign Supply claims it started selling them in 1986.

also.quote: Florida-based National Campaign Supply claims to have started selling them in 1986.

events.notes: Company claim relayed by Time; the company's own site returned an empty page to curl. Keep 'says' or 'claims'.

events.claim: Janet Boudreau drew the oval "I Voted" sticker with a rippling American flag in 1987, soon after she bought the election supply company Intab from her father for a dollar. It became one of Intab's best sellers.
events.quote: Boudreau created her “I Voted” design in 1987, soon after becoming president and owner of Intab, an election supply business she purchased from her father for a single dollar.

also.quote: At the time, the business was based in Seattle
Little did she know, the hand-drawn “I Voted sticker” — one of the first five products Boudreau created — would go on to become a top seller for all 28 years she ran the company.
"I wanted them to see people with an 'I Voted' sticker and think, 'Oh, I should do that,'" she says.
She designed the iconic sticker that has been a polling place staple for decades: a simple ellipse featuring a rippling red, white and blue American flag.

events.notes: AARP (Grace Dickinson, Oct 23, 2024). PATENT: no record. Google Patents returns nothing for inventor Janet Boudreau (only an unrelated 2005 staple extractor by Wendy Janet Boudreau) or assignee Intab / Independent Tabulation. Never say 'patented'. COPYRIGHT: Boudreau is quoted, 'Others claim to have created that design, but I copyrighted it long ago' (Washington Examiner, 2024), and Hyperallergic says she 'had the design copyrighted'; no Copyright Office record was checked. Say 'Boudreau says she copyrighted it' if used. Place: AARP says Intab was then in Seattle; Intab today lists P.O. Box 186, Morrisville, NC. She sold Intab in 2015 to two employees (AARP). Also her earlier sighting: AARP says she had seen only one earlier sticker, black-and-white with a checkmark and an X.

events.claim: Boudreau remembers first seeing her flag sticker everywhere in 1988. By 2000, she says, Intab was selling more than 100 million "I Voted" stickers in each even-numbered election year, to nearly all 50 states.
events.quote: By 2000, Intab was selling more than 100 million “I Voted” stickers in every midterm and general election year, and distributed them to nearly, if not all, 50 states, Boudreau says.

also.quote: Janet Boudreau remembers back in 1988 when she first started seeing the rippling flag “I Voted” sticker popping up at election time.
Boudreau had the design copyrighted , and by late 1988, the stickers were available in all 50 states.
The company sells more than 30 million stickers per year, according to the San Jose Mercury News .

events.notes: SALES CONFLICT: AARP (her own account) says >100 million 'in every midterm and general election year' by 2000. Midterm and presidential years alternate, so that is per even year, i.e. roughly every two years, NOT 'annually'. The research's 'over 100 million annually by 2000' is wrong. A separate 2014 San Jose Mercury News figure (via the Examiner) says >30 million per year, a different era and owner; don't merge the two. 50 STATES CONFLICT: 'all 50 states by (late) 1988' is in Hyperallergic, citing a WFMY page that blocked every tool; Boudreau herself (AARP) says only 'nearly, if not all, 50 states' by 2000. Use AARP's wording.

events.claim: In a 2006 Michigan primary experiment, a mailer listing whether the recipient and their neighbors had voted raised turnout by 8.1 percentage points over households that got no mail, where turnout was 29.7 percent.
events.quote: Mailing a household’s own voting record resulted in a 4.9 percentage point increase and listing neighbors’ voting records resulted in an 8.1 percentage point increase in turnout among registered voters.

also.quote: The other three treatment groups also voted at a higher rate than the comparison group, where turnout was 29.7 percent.
Substantially higher turnout was observed among those who received mailings promising to publicize their turnout to their household or their neighbors.

events.notes: Gerber, Green & Larimer, 'Social Pressure and Voter Turnout: Evidence from a Large-Scale Field Experiment', American Political Science Review 102(1):33-48, Feb 2008 (Crossref; abstract read). The paper's full text was not read (Yale ISPS PDF link serves an HTML page); the 8.1-point and 29.7% figures come from J-PAL's summary of the study, a research organization, so the number is near-primary. Study is about mailers, not stickers; use only as context for social pressure.

events.claim: In 2008 Starbucks and Ben & Jerry's dropped plans to give free coffee and ice cream only to people with an "I voted" sticker and offered them to everyone, after a reminder that election laws bar rewarding people for voting. Krispy Kreme kept its sticker offer.
events.quote: Election laws say you cannot give people free stuff to encourage them or dissuade them from voting, and a Washington state official made that point yesterday. So some other companies, Starbucks and Ben and Jerry's, modified their offers.

also.quote: And if you're still hungry, then you can go to Krispy Kreme.
On Tuesday November 8, participating locations will be doling out free doughnuts to all visitors sporting their 'I Voted' stickers.

events.notes: NPR Morning Edition, Nov 4, 2008 (Steve Inskeep). The research's claim that Krispy Kreme also changed its offer in 2008 is NOT supported: NPR says Krispy Kreme was offering doughnuts to sticker wearers and sends listeners there. In 2016 Krispy Kreme again offered free doughnuts to sticker wearers (Refinery29, secondary). In 2020 news reports say Krispy Kreme gave a doughnut to anyone, no sticker needed (not read directly). The 'Washington state official' is not named in the transcript.

events.claim: On Election Day 2010, Facebook showed 61 million U.S. users a message with an "I Voted" button and photos of friends who had clicked it. The researchers estimated it brought out about 60,000 voters directly and 280,000 more through friends, about 340,000 in all, and close friends did most of the spreading.
events.quote: Our results suggest that the Facebook social message increased turnout directly by about 60,000 voters and indirectly through social contagion by another 280,000 voters, for a total of 340,000 additional votes.

also.quote: The effect of social transmission on real-world voting was greater than the direct effect of the messages themselves, and nearly all the transmission occurred between ‘close friends’ who were more likely to have a face-to-face relationship.
Finally, we used a group-level process to study the validated voting behaviour of 6.3 million users matched to publicly available voter records (see Supplementary Information).
Similarly, the difference in voting between those who received the social message and those who received the informational message was 0.39%

events.notes: Bond, Fariss, Jones, Kramer, Marlow, Settle & Fowler, 'A 61-million-person experiment in social influence and political mobilization', Nature 489(7415):295-298, published online Sept 12, 2012, doi:10.1038/nature11421 (confirmed via Crossref). Effect is measured on validated votes in a 6.3 million-user matched sample, then scaled. The share of 'I Voted' clickers who did not actually vote is NOT in the main paper text (probably the Supplementary Information, not read): leave it out. Nature's news piece was not found. The Examiner's 'turnout increased by 0.6%' is a garble; don't use it. The 0.39% is social vs informational message, not informational vs control.

events.claim: Since at least 2014, voters have left "I Voted" stickers on Susan B. Anthony's grave in Mount Hope Cemetery. As many as 12,000 people visited on Election Day 2016.
events.quote: On Election Day 2016, as many as 12,000 people made the trek to Anthony’s final resting place to honor the work she did to win women the right to vote, and to mark the first time people could cast a vote for a female major-party presidential candidate, Hillary Clinton.

also.quote: Rochester women have been coming to Anthony’s grave with flowers and stickers since at least 2014.
Potential for over 10,000 visitors on November 5, 2024 (there will be a line to visit Susan B. Anthony’s grave)

events.notes: Rochester Democrat and Chronicle via USA Today, Marcia Greenwood, Oct 26, 2020 (read in Chrome; curl blocked). Smithsonian Magazine (Erin Blakemore, April 20, 2016, updated Oct 28, 2020) read through the Wayback Machine because smithsonianmag.com returned 403. '12,000' is 'as many as', not a count.

events.claim: Chicago had stopped giving out stickers about a decade earlier because voters stuck them on water fountains, windows and doors at polling places, and custodians spent hours scraping them off. For 2016 it ordered a million Tyvek wristbands reading "I Voted! Did You?" for about $19,000, or 1.9 cents each.
events.quote: The bands cost the city about $19,000 or 1.9 cents each for the million they ordered.

also.quote: They stuck stickers to water fountains, to windows, to doors, to door frames.
The slogan is also printed—in smaller point size—in Spanish, Chinese and Hindi, the three languages required in Chicago by Section. 203 of the Voting Rights Act.

events.notes: electionline Weekly, Oct 13, 2016 (Mindy Moretti), quoting Chicago board spokesman James P. Allen. Before the wristbands Chicago handed out a paper receipt. Chicago's return to stickers: board minutes show the switch began in 2021 (see mail-stickers-chicago-2022 and chicago-2021-sticker-contract). The Chicago Tribune 2024-03-15 story was not read.

events.claim: In 2017 New York City's Campaign Finance Board picked a new sticker by public ranked vote. Marie Dagata and Scott Heinz of Bronxville won with colored subway lines crossing the O in I Voted, chosen from more than 700 entries and nearly 10,000 ballots, and it debuted at the September 12 primary.
events.quote: The winning sticker features multi-colored subway lines crossing over the “O” in “I Voted.” The image, designed by Marie Dagata and Scott Heinz of Bronxville, N.Y., won out over nine other finalists in the “I Voted” sticker contest run by the NYC Campaign Finance Board, the group announced Thursday.

also.quote: The CFB received more than 700 submissions in April and wrote on their site that "nearly 10,000 'ballots' were cast via phones, computers or tablets."
"All the people of the boroughs meet together, pass each other, need each other in the subway and the voting booth." - Marie Dagata, 59, and Scott Heinz, 56, from Bronxville, NY

events.notes: Research phrase 'subway-line circles' is loose; sources describe subway lines crossing the O. NYC's first contest (2013) was won by 10-year-old Zoe Markman with a Statue of Liberty design (WNYC). Spell Dagata (one outlet has 'Dagarta').

events.claim: For the 2018 elections, Alaska's Division of Elections worked with an Alaskan artist on stickers showing Alaskan animals, including a moose, walrus, raven, crab, eagle, caribou and beaver. The stickers were also produced in Alaska Native languages, and the set won a 2019 EAC award.
events.quote: Inspired, the elections office worked with an Alaskan artist to produce stickers for the 2018 elections with various Alaskan animals. Stickers included the moose, walrus, raven, Dungeness crab, king crab, eagle, caribou, and beaver.
events.notes: The release says 'Alaska’s Native Language' (singular) without naming languages; do not list specific languages for 2018. Artist not named on this page. The EAC's individual 2019 Alaska award page now returns 404.

events.claim: Washoe County updated its sticker in 2018 alongside new voting machines. The design shows the Sierra mountains behind the city skyline, and it won a 2019 EAC award.
events.quote: The sticker features the Sierra mountains in the background and the city skyline to celebrate civic pride and the countys picturesque landscape.

also.quote: In 2018, in conjunction with the introduction of new county-wide election machinery, Washoe County updated their I Voted sticker.

events.notes: Research said Washoe won 'in 2019' for a Sierra design: correct for the award (2019 Clearies), but the sticker itself dates to 2018.

events.claim: In 2019 the U.S. Election Assistance Commission added a category for original and creative I Voted stickers to its annual Clearie awards, judged on creativity, originality, artistry and local flair. The first five winners, announced in January 2020, were Alaska, Clark County NV, Douglas County NV, Louisiana and Washoe County NV.
events.quote: This year’s EAC Clearinghouse Awards competition will accept submissions for a special new category: original and creative “I voted” stickers.

also.quote: Alaska; Clark County, NV; Douglas County, NV; Louisiana; and Washoe County, NV were recognized for their civic-minded and patriotic renditions of the “I Voted” sticker.

events.notes: The EAC blog also says the sticker 'Started in the early 1980s'; that is the EAC's own framing, not a sourced origin date. The press release calls stickers 'an inexpensive way' to show pride but gives no price.

events.claim: San Mateo County found that mail voters were dropping off ballots in person just to get a sticker. In November 2019 it piloted putting an I Voted sticker in every mailed ballot package, repeated it in 2020, and added a shareable digital sticker.
events.quote: “I Voted” stickers are so popular that many of our permanent Vote by Mail voters were dropping their ballots off at Vote Centers just to obtain their stickers.

also.quote: The Elections Division for San Mateo County, California conducted a pilot program in November 2019 to include an I Voted sticker inside the Official Ballot package sent to all registered voters.

events.notes: The PDF is the county's own award submission hosted by the EAC.

events.claim: Alaska's 2020 stickers used four designs by Alaskan artist Barbara Lavallee showing Alaskan women, in English, Spanish, Tagalog and seven Alaska Native languages. Voters who voted from home could download digital versions.
events.quote: The stickerswereavailable in English, Spanish, Koyukon, Gwichin, Aleut, Tagalog, Alutiiq, Northern Inupiaq, Nunivak Cupig, and Yup'ik. For those who votedfrom home, digital stickerswereavailable for download on the Divisions website so voters could display that they exercised their right to vote.

also.quote: Created by beloved Alaskan artist, Barbara Lavallee, the stickers feature her stylized depiction of the diversity, strength, and power of Alaskanwomen.Thefour uniquestickerdesignswere colorful and well received.

events.notes: Ten languages confirmed: English, Spanish, Koyukon, Gwich'in, Aleut, Tagalog, Alutiiq, Northern Inupiaq, Nunivak Cup'ig, Yup'ik. The EAC page drops spaces and apostrophes (quoted as rendered); spell Gwich'in and Cup'ig correctly in page copy. This was an Honorable Mention, not a winner. elections.alaska.gov/Core/ElectionStickers.php returned a human-verification wall (curl 405) and a TLS error to WebFetch; not read.

events.claim: In October 2020 the Friends of Mount Hope Cemetery put clear plastic sleeves over the headstones of Susan B. Anthony and her sister, after a spring restoration showed sticker glue and the solvents used to remove it had damaged the marble. Visitors now put their stickers on the cover.
events.quote: During a springtime restoration project, it became clear that the fragile marble marker had sustained damage from a combination of adhesive residue and the solvents and methods needed to remove it, Patricia Corcoran, president of nonprofit Friends of Mount Hope Cemetery, wrote in an email.

also.quote: As a result, the group had clear plastic sleeves made for Anthony’s headstone and that of her sister, Mary S. Anthony, for use during election season, and people can put their "I Voted" stickers on the sleeves.
Susan B. Anthony’s grave marker has a clear cover to prevent damage. “I voted” stickers may be placed on the cover.

events.notes: Damage-related: yes, per the cemetery group's president. Sleeves were in place by the first day of early voting in 2020 (late October). The cover is seasonal ('for use during election season'), not permanent. FOMH page dated Oct 29, 2024.

events.claim: A 2020 paper by religious-studies scholar Jordan Conley in the Journal of Feminist Studies in Religion compares the stickers left at Anthony's grave to votive offerings.
events.quote: Voting, Votive, Devotion: “I Voted” Stickers and Ritualization at Susan B. Anthony's Grave

also.quote: Journal of Feminist Studies in Religion, vol. 36, no. 2, pp. 43-62 (2020)

events.notes: Bibliographic details confirmed via Crossref and Wikidata (Q128267120); the article text (Project MUSE, paywalled) was not read, so describe only its title and topic. Wikipedia's summary (Asclepius comparison, 2016 and 2018 elections) is unread secondary: don't repeat it.

events.claim: Voters who vote from home or abroad can often get a digital sticker instead. Alaska made its 2020 stickers downloadable, Oregon offers virtual stickers such as I Voted (The Oregon Way), Cuyahoga County, Ohio posts one for mail voters, and the federal FVAP site makes I Voted From stickers for overseas voters by country.
events.quote: For those who votedfrom home, digital stickerswereavailable for download on the Divisions website so voters could display that they exercised their right to vote.

also.quote: I Voted (virtual sticker)
If you're voting in U.S. elections from another country, let your friends and family know with your very own "I Voted From" sticker.
Click the I Voted! sticker below, save it, and share it on your social media to show your fellow Ohioans that you voted by mail and made your voice heard!
Commemorative Suffragist Digital "I Voted" Stickers Click on the image to read, download or print.

events.notes: Oregon quote is from build/state-facts/or.json (verified there), not re-read today. San Mateo also made a digital sticker (see mail-stickers-sanmateo-2019). Colorado runs a digital sticker contest shown in BallotTrax messages (co.json). Connecticut's suffrage-centennial digital stickers were started by Wilton designer Pamela Hovland (Yale faculty).

events.claim: Several Nashville polling places ran out of a special sticker for the August 6, 2020 election, designed by high school senior Milka Negasi for the women's suffrage centennial. Metro Arts posted a free downloadable version for non-commercial use.
events.quote: During the August 6 election, several polling locations ran out of the popular sticker, designed by Hume-Fogg Academic Magnet High School senior Milka Negasi to commemorate the Women's Suffrage Centennial.

also.quote: Until then, we're offering a downloadable version for you to print and enjoy—non-commercially—in celebration of voting rights.
The contest received 75 entries, which a citizen selection panel narrowed down to 8 finalists. More than 2,300 Nashvillians voted for their favorite sticker.

events.notes: Metro Arts Nashville with the Davidson County Election Commission; contest open to Davidson County students in grades 7 to 12.

events.claim: St. Louis County's first sticker contest, run with the county library in 2021, produced three new stickers plus a bonus I Voted at Home sticker drawn by 11-year-old Julia Boren, whose entry included a mailbox. It goes out with absentee ballots and was first used in the April 5, 2022 election.
events.quote: As a bonus, the BOE also got a new "I Voted at Home" sticker when the artwork from eleven-year-old Julia Boren included a mailbox in the design in her hand drawn entry. The design is now included with absentee ballots mailed to St. Louis County voters.

also.quote: The contest, by design, resulted in three new I Voted stickers for 2022; a bonus sticker for voters voting by absentee ballot; and a new social media campaign featuring the stickers targeted to voters under age 35.

events.notes: Source: Board of Elections 2021-2022 Biennial Report, pp. 11-12. Other winners: Mariam Rana (grade 6), Tara Wang (Pattonville High), Kathryn Owens (adult). The report says the county's first sticker debuted in 2006 and off-the-shelf stickers were used from 2016.

events.claim: Smithsonian political history curator Claire Jerry said the museum's oldest Election Day item is a 1920 button and ribbon reading I cast my first vote on November 2nd, 1920. She doubted stickers still drive turnout but noted parents sharing stickers with their children.
events.quote: “I don't think it mobilizes people to go vote anymore — I don't know if we could ever measure if it actually had that effect,” she said.

also.quote: “The oldest Election day paraphernalia we have is from 1920, during the women’s suffrage movement,” Jerry told Hyperallergic.
“The oldest Election day paraphernalia we have is from 1920, during the women’s suffrage movement,” Jerry told Hyperallergic.

events.notes: The 'Current, 2022' piece in the research is a reprint of Hyperallergic (Nov 7, 2022); it still says 'told Hyperallergic'. Cite Hyperallergic. Her quote contains an em dash; render without it if paraphrasing. Hyperallergic is an interview with the curator, so it is near-primary for her words but secondary for facts.

events.claim: Chicago dropped stickers around 2016 for paper wristbands. In 2021 its board switched an existing wristband contract to I Voted stickers, and in 2022 a commissioner put on record that stickers were chosen because they fit into vote-by-mail envelopes more easily.
events.quote: Commissioner Kresse wanted to put on the record that we are not going with wristbands, but with the “I Voted” stickers because the stickers can be inserted into Vote-by-Mail envelopes much easier.

also.quote: Executive Director explained that the contracted product would now be “I Voted” stickers, not wristbands as was the product originally under this contract.
Second, we finalized our design for this year’s “I Voted” stickers.

events.notes: This dates Chicago's return to stickers to 2021-2022, earlier than the March 2024 Tribune story suggests; the 2024 piece covers a redesign (artist Jane Ignacio per secondary Hoodline, which is AI-assisted and not used). Parent has the 2016 wristband sources.

events.claim: Pima County had put English I Voted Early stickers in ballot-by-mail packets before 2021. In 2022 it introduced one trilingual sticker in English, Tohono O'odham and Spanish for early voters by mail or in person.
events.quote: Before 2021, the Pima County Recorder’s Office included only the English “I Voted Early” stickers in ballot-by-mail packets.

also.quote: The sticker reads “I voted” in English, “A:ñi ‘ant wodalt” in Tohono O’odham and “Yo Voté” in Spanish.

events.notes: recorder.pima.gov/IVotedSticker returned 403; the July 13, 2022 memo PDF was read.

events.claim: In 2022 election officials were warned that a tight paper supply could affect everything from ballots to I Voted stickers. An EAC paper supply alert told offices to order stickers at least four months ahead, and Chicago's 2022 printing renewal, which included stickers, cost about 20 percent more because of raw material prices.
events.quote: Order “I Voted” stickers at least 4 months in advance of the election

also.quote: elections officials from across the country meeting under heightened security in swing state Wisconsin were urged to prepare for supply chain issues that could lead to shortages in paper used for everything from ballots to I voted stickers for years to come.
Ms. Walls mentioned that there is a twenty-percent increase in the contract amount over the last amount due to increases in the cost of raw materials, for example, paper, the, toner and ink.

events.notes: AP story body talks about ballots, inserts and envelopes; stickers appear only in the AP photo caption (quoted). The EAC alert PDF is dated March 30, 2022 (PDF metadata) and is advice, not a report of an actual shortage. No source read reports a jurisdiction that actually ran short of stickers or changed size because of the 2022 paper crunch (Monroe County NY's smaller 2023 stickers were an ordering error). A Stateline story reportedly quoting Jim Suver on stickers was blocked (403) and not read.

events.claim: Ulster County Election Commissioner Ashley Dittus opened Rowan's emailed entry first and championed it. For the 2022 midterm the Board of Elections had 100,000 of his stickers for about 90,000 expected voters and told poll workers to give one per person.
events.quote: The Ulster County Board of Elections is expecting 90,000 voters this election season Each voter will go home with one "I Voted" sticker designed by Hudson Rowan The BOE has 100,000 stickers waiting for those participating in the midterm elections

also.quote: “We’re telling the election inspectors ‘one per person!’ We have to make sure we control the sticker distribution so that we don’t run out and that everybody will have their chance to have it,” said Dittus.

Recently, our office was contacted by the U.S. Election Assistance Commission to partner on a collaboration to encourage other election officials across the country to launch similar programs of their own, all thanks to you and your colorful creation.”

events.notes: Dittus (D) and John Quigley (R) are the two Ulster County election commissioners (HV1). Spectrum's 'What You Need To Know' bullets are run together in the page text; quote as bullets if used.

events.claim: In a 2018 randomized test of get-out-the-vote texts run by Vote.org, texts that linked to a digital "I Voted" sticker for Facebook raised turnout 0.25 percentage points; the standard text raised it 0.24 points. The two effects were indistinguishable.
events.quote: The Digital Sticker treatment generated an increase in turnout of 0.25 percentage points at a cost per net vote of $89.12 (11.2 net votes/$1000).

also.quote: Both treatments generated significant increases in turnout, and the size of the treatment effects was indistinguishable.
The Digital Sticker treatment allowed an easy link from the SMS message to posting a digital “I Voted” sticker on Facebook.

events.notes: Memo 004 of Vote.org's 2018 cold SMS program, summarized by Debra Cleaver (VoteAmerica, Oct 1, 2019); evaluations by Christopher B. Mann (with Katherine Haenschen on some memos). A nonprofit research memo, not peer-reviewed; memo PDF itself not read. Sample size not confirmed: leave it out.

events.claim: A repeat of the Facebook experiment in the 2012 presidential election (Jones et al., PLOS ONE, 2017) again found a small rise in voting, estimated at about 270,000 more voters including close friends.
events.quote: The treatment effects also spread through the network as in 2010, causing an additional 180,000 close friends of the treated to vote as well, for a total increase of 270,000 people voting in the 2012 U.S. Presidential Election.

also.quote: This yields an estimated treatment effect of +0.24% (95% CI +0.03% to +0.44%) that is unlikely to be due to chance ( p = 0.0266).

events.notes: The unadjusted estimate (+0.17%) was not significant; the +0.24% adds 2010 vote history as a control. Say 'small', don't headline the number.

events.claim: For a student election at Blewett, a St. Louis public school, on October 29, 1920, the school print shop printed "I have voted" tags, enough to give each student one as he voted. 1,250 students registered and 1,170 (94%) voted, the St. Louis Board of Education reported.

law.claim: Federal law makes it a crime to make or offer an expenditure to anyone to vote or not vote, or to vote for or against a candidate.
law.quote: Whoever makes or offers to make an expenditure to any person, either to vote or withhold his vote, or to vote for or against any candidate; and Whoever solicits, accepts, or receives any such expenditure in consideration of his vote or the withholding of his vote—

also.quote: Shall be fined under this title or imprisoned not more than one year, or both; and if the violation was willful, shall be fined under this title or imprisoned not more than two years, or both.
or pays or offers to pay or accepts payment either for registration to vote or for voting shall be fined not more than $10,000 or imprisoned not more than five years, or both

law.notes: Text from Cornell LII (uscode.house.gov returned a stub page to curl). 52 U.S.C. 10307(c) applies only to elections with a federal candidate on the ballot. Neither statute mentions stickers; the link to freebies is the DOJ and state guidance below.

law.claim: The Justice Department lists paying voters to vote in elections with a federal candidate on the ballot as a federal election crime, citing both laws above.
law.quote: Paying voters to register to vote, or to vote in elections where a federal candidate’s name is on the ballot (52 U.S.C. § 10307(c), 18 U.S.C. § 597)

also.quote: Paying voters to register to vote, or to vote in elections where a federal candidate's name is on the ballot (52 U.S.C. § 10307(c), 18 U.S.C. § 597)

law.notes: Read in the U.S. Attorney's Office, Western District of Louisiana fact sheet PDF (justice.gov, Oct 31, 2022). The New Hampshire office's version (requested in the research) returned no readable text to curl or WebFetch; its matching wording comes from a search extract only. DOJ's manual 'Federal Prosecution of Election Offenses' (8th ed., Dec 2017) was not read. Neither source mentions stickers.

law.claim: Wisconsin's Elections Commission says businesses that give food or discounts to people with an "I Voted" sticker are breaking the state's election bribery law, which bars offering anything worth more than $1 to get someone to vote. Giveaways near polls must be open to everyone, voted or not.
law.quote: “Every election, well-meaning businesses or groups offer discounts or free food and drinks to people who come into their establishment with an I Voted sticker,” said Meagan Wolfe, Wisconsin’s chief election official. “However, that is against the law.”

also.quote: According to state law against election bribery, it is illegal to offer someone an item worth more than $1.00 to induce a person to vote, not vote, vote for a particular candidate, not vote for a particular candidate, or vote a specific way in a referendum.
Any items being given away must be available to everyone whether they have voted or not.

law.notes: Commission news release, Oct 29, 2020. No newer version found; check elections.wi.gov before publishing if describing current policy.

law.claim: Illinois law says that if an election authority gives polling places stickers to hand to voters, no one who has voted can be denied one. The rule took effect June 1, 2015, and at least one election office stopped giving stickers rather than risk running out.
law.quote: If an election authority provides each polling place with stickers or emblems to be given to voters indicating that the person has voted, no person who has voted shall be denied such sticker or emblem.

also.quote: So we chose not to give 'I Voted' stickers thinking that if we would accidentally run out, we would actually be breaking that new law," she said.

law.notes: 10 ILCS 5/17-8, last sentence; added by Public Act 98-1171, effective June 1, 2015. Read in the full Election Code on ilga.gov in Chrome (ilga.gov blocks curl); 17-8 is the only section of the Code that mentions stickers. WGLT (March 15, 2016) quotes Cathie Haab, Bloomington Election Commission. A 2025 bill (SB1576) to create an 'I Voted' Sticker Commission was re-referred to Assignments and is not law.
